item.title: After digitizing stacks of my old CDs to lossless audio, I finally perfected my ripping workflow
item.itunes:title: After digitizing stacks of my old CDs to lossless audio, I finally perfected my ripping workflow
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I started getting into the groove of ripping my CDs to lossless audio to replace my enormous collection of crappy, low-quality MP3s. Years ago, I was ripping discs to smaller files to save space on MP3 players. I don't need to worry about that anymore, and I want to put high-quality FLAC rips on my self-hosted media servers like Jellyfin and Plex.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

It gives me a huge audio upgrade and lets me listen to my music the way it was meant to be heard. I typically select an album on my TV and play it through my AV receiver system. During the new ripping process, I've found ways to make it quick and efficient while maintaining quality audio from my CD rips.

Ripping CDs again

It brings back memories, but I was doing it wrong

Ripping CDs again brings back fond memories of using free tools like Windows Media Player, MusicMatch, and iTunes. Windows Media Player would rip CDs to WMA, and iTunes to AAC. At the time, neither offered FLAC. However, each also offered lossless audio versions. For instance, iTunes supported ALAC (saved as M4A), plus uncompressed WAV and AIFF. WMP also offered WMA Lossless and uncompressed WAV. But neither tool offered lossless by default.

These formats weren't universal, causing compatibility issues. Apple's iPod couldn't natively play WMA, and Microsoft's Zune (if you remember it) didn't play Apple's ALAC format. MP3 was popular because it's small and widely compatible across platforms. FLAC was a better alternative for archiving music because it's open-source and uses lossless compression. It isn't dependent on one company's software ecosystem.

At the time, however, everyone was ripping CDs to low-quality MP3s to save bandwidth and storage on our devices. We also tricked ourselves into thinking MP3s, even under 320 kbps, sounded good. We worried about how many songs we could fit on a device, not the true immersive sound quality of our music.

Plus, Napster and the file-sharing craze were around, and internet speeds weren't very fast. This time, I am ripping to FLAC to keep an open, lossless master copy, so I can keep the original audio intact and create compatible copies if needed. I have hundreds of discs, many I forgot about, and I want to digitize my music collection the right way.

I thought all Blu-ray drives were the same until I found the perfect one for ripping physical media to Plex

All Blu-ray drives aren't created equal when you're backing up 4K movies for self-hosted media servers.

By  Brian Burgess

The right software for CD ripping workflow

I went for quality audio with a burst of speed

When I started my ripping project, I used dBpoweramp since it is designed for a large workload of CD rips. However, it is trialware and is close to $50 after that. I needed something fast, free, and accurate to make the tedious process a cinch. So I went back to Exact Audio Copy (EAC), since it's freeware and produces high-quality FLAC rips. I've used it to rip discs before, but I found settings that made my workflow easier.

For instance, using the "Copy Selected Tracks" option instead of "Test & Copy Selected Tracks" prevents multiple passes before ripping. I also set the extraction method to "Burst mode" under drive options, which keeps the ripping process to 10 minutes or less, depending on the CD. I also set it to eject the disc automatically after the rip completes. That way, I can remove the disc, put it in its case, and pop the next one back in.

Another useful option is to have it automatically use the AccurateRip metadata engine to find the disc's information, like artist, album, track names, and cover art. If that doesn't work, I can use the CUETools DB Metadata Plugin or MusicBrainz to look up the details. I've found that AccurateRip retrieves album data the fastest. But sometimes I need to use extensive search settings in CUETools if a disc is rare or the other database plugins can't find the correct info.

I also set EAC to rip directly to an external drive so I can put the FLAC files on my self-hosted media server platforms. I am still organizing where I want each album to go. Ripping once to an external drive lets me choose where to put my music. I can plug the drive into my Raspberry Pi jukebox, put some albums on my other devices, and keep my library archived.

Exact Audio Copy
See at MajorGeeks

Playing lossless music

Quality audio through my AV receiver and other devices

EAC does a fabulous job making a tedious task easier. It found the disc metadata right away, ripped it quickly in burst mode, and popped the finished CD out so I could add a new one. I used a 1 TB external drive, so I didn't need to worry about the larger size of FLAC files. Even after what seemed like the 1,000th disc, I had plenty of room.

After the ripping was complete, I added files to my self-hosted media servers, other drives, and devices. My main AV receiver is connected to my TV, where I listen most often. I use Plex or Jellyfin to sort through albums and playlists and find and play what I want. I also use Jellybox or Plexamp to download music to my phone for offline listening.

With high-quality files, listening to my old CDs feels like rediscovering something new. I hear sounds, effects, even lyrics I hadn't heard before. Instead of the crappy MP3s I'd given up on, I have a new, fully immersive music collection. Plus, I don't have to worry about scratching discs or putting them back into the right case.

I turned Jellyfin into the Spotify alternative I've always wanted with this app

I can play music from Jellyfin, but this app makes it feel like my own Spotify.

7
By  Brian Burgess

A CD ripping audio upgrade workflow that works best

It had been ages since I ripped a CD when I first started this project. Now, after ripping stacks of them, I finally found the best workflow for me. Sometimes discs are too damaged to read, but EAC can usually get them working if I use the right settings and allow for patience. Overall, I can't complain about the speed or the improved audio quality of my re-ripped CD library, which is accessible everywhere.

item.title: Ethernet beats Wi-Fi where it counts, and you can run cables without drilling a single hole
item.itunes:title: Ethernet beats Wi-Fi where it counts, and you can run cables without drilling a single hole
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Wi-Fi is omnipresent in 2026, with Wi-Fi 7 routers and devices hogging much of the conversations around home networking. While modern high-speed internet and Wi-Fi 7 hardware may have solved the speed component of the equation, Ethernet still wins when it comes to reliability. A direct line between the router and a high-priority device doesn't depend on free and unhindered airwaves.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That said, running cables is as annoying as they say. Routing them inside the walls or drilling holes isn't the most convenient, but there are simpler alternatives. You can choose flat LAN cables and run them along your walls or ditch them entirely in favor of pre-installed coaxial cables or powerline adapters. These alternatives aren't always inferior in practice, giving you the benefits of a wired connection without the hassle.

I decided I didn't need Ethernet everywhere, and my home network didn't fall apart

Modern Wi-Fi is surprisingly capable for almost every device in your house

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Wi-Fi has come a long way, but wired is wired

Wi-Fi has fundamental drawbacks compared to Ethernet

Over the years, successive Wi-Fi standards have tried to make wireless connections as reliable as wired ones. Wi-Fi 6 brought bidirectional MU-MIMO and a significant throughput boost, while Wi-F 6E introduced the 6 GHz band for minimized interference. Then, Wi-Fi 7 brought another massive speed boost along with 320 MHz channels and Multi-Link Operation.

Today, high-speed internet is more common than ever and even multi-gig plans aren't rare anymore. While Wi-Fi 7 has removed the limits on peak wireless speeds and reduced congestion and interference, it's still subject to the quirks of wireless networks. Wi-Fi is inherently a shared medium, and competing access points and devices are still a problem. Speed is just one aspect of a decent home network; you also need rock-solid reliability.

This is where Ethernet is still king, thanks to the absence of congestion and interference. There are no competing neighbors, dead zones, or legacy 2.4 GHz devices creating interference, range, or airtime issues. Unlike Wi-Fi, Ethernet is a full-duplex medium, allowing simultaneous transmission in both directions.

The devices that need 24/7 reliability perform best on a wired connection, so your gaming PC, smart TV, streaming device, or game console benefit greatly from Ethernet. Wherever possible, it's best to arrange LAN cable runs, so you can eliminate wireless shenanigans.

CableGeeker Cat6 Flat Ethernet Cable

The CableGeeker Cat6 Flat Ethernet cable is a high-performance cable that supports fast and reliable data transfer for gaming. It features a flat design that reduces tangling while also saving you space and a durable structure that combines PVC and twisted cores for durability. This Cat6 cable has a high bandwidth of up to 500 MHz and 10 Gbps. 

See at Amazon
Why I insist on Ethernet on my PC even when it's a pain to set up

Ethernet beats Wi-Fi hands down, and is worth a few hassles

36
By  Tanveer Singh

Routing cable through walls isn't always easy, but you don't need to do that

Secured cable runs can be just as effective

Bringing an Ethernet connection to every room in the house can be a considerable undertaking. You often need to have the skill and time to route cables internally through the walls, which isn't always possible. In rented houses, it's not even a question of time and money; it may not be allowed. The good news is that you have feasible alternatives that can work just as well.

Most homes might already have Cat5e cables routed internally to one or more rooms, which are enough for Gigabit connections. You don't need to install new cables just because you moved to a new house. For multi-gig plans, you'll need Cat6 or Cat6a cables, but most people aren't running such high-speed plans.

If your house doesn't have pre-installed cables, you could pick a flat Cat6a cable and run it along the baseboards or the ceiling. You can use nail clips to secure the cable and hide it under the carpet or out of sight along the ceiling. Shorter runs to separate access points can reduce eyesore while providing Ethernet as well as reliable Wi-Fi to every room. You don't need to hire anyone for the job either, making the cable run much simpler and cost-effective.

Weight
0.7 Kilograms
Speed
Up to 2.5 Gbps

Ready to up your network game? Use nothing but existing coaxial cabling and two of these to create an Ethernet-like link between rooms. 2.5GbE and PoE support ensure you have ample features to transform your home LAN.

See at Amazon
Your house can have Ethernet everywhere, and here's how I did it without drilling a single hole

Renters rejoice!

23
By  Ty Sherback

MoCA and powerline adapters can eliminate cable runs entirely

Where there's a will, there's a way

Depending on your house, you might not even have to install LAN cables. Many homes have pre-installed coaxial cables for TVs. These cables often go unused as people switch to streaming apps. MoCA can provide you with Gigabit Ethernet via these coaxial cables, eliminating the need to invest in and route new cables. Coaxial cables are already there and all you need is a pair of MoCA adapters to get going.

MoCA 2.5 adapters are even capable of 2.5 GbE connections, so multi-gig users should also take notice. MoCA can even coexist with your TV signal because they run at different frequencies. MoCA is still half-duplex, so it's not a 1:1 Ethernet replacement, but that's a small drawback considering the convenience.

If you don't have coaxial cables inside your walls, you can use a pair of powerline adapters to run Ethernet signals through your power cables. Powerline connections are prone to electrical interference from heavy appliances, so latency can spike when they are turned on. Also, your adapters and the PC need to be on the same electrical phase to avoid speed degradation.

Powerline connections offer significantly reduced speeds compared to what your internet plan is rated for, but if your max speeds are high enough, it can be a perfectly serviceable solution.

TP-Link AV2000 Powerline Ethernet Adapter
See at Amazon
I'd do these 5 things differently if I were setting up my home network from scratch

I don't have the most efficient home network, but I intend to change that the next time

2
By  Tanveer Singh

Getting Ethernet doesn't always need a ton of effort

Running cables through walls is usually the preferred method to route LAN connections to your high-speed devices, but there are always simpler alternatives. You could run flat cables along the walls or use MoCA or powerline adapters to eliminate new cables entirely. Each solution has its downsides, but they can be just what you need in the right scenario.

While modern high-speed internet and Wi-Fi 7 hardware may have solved the speed component of the equation, Ethernet still wins when it comes to reliability. A direct line between the router and a high-priority device doesn't depend on free and unhindered airwaves.

That said, running cables is as annoying as they say. Routing them inside the walls or drilling holes isn't the most convenient, but there are simpler alternatives. You can choose flat LAN cables and run them along your walls or ditch them entirely in favor of pre-installed coaxial cables or powerline adapters. These alternatives aren't always inferior in practice, giving you the benefits of a wired connection without the hassle.

I decided I didn't need Ethernet everywhere, and my home network didn't fall apart

By  Tanveer Singh

Wi-Fi has come a long way, but wired is wired

Wi-Fi has fundamental drawbacks compared to Ethernet

Over the years, successive Wi-Fi standards have tried to make wireless connections as reliable as wired ones. Wi-Fi 6 brought bidirectional MU-MIMO and a significant throughput boost, while Wi-F 6E introduced the 6 GHz band for minimized interference. Then, Wi-Fi 7 brought another massive speed boost along with 320 MHz channels and Multi-Link Operation.

Today, high-speed internet is more common than ever and even multi-gig plans aren't rare anymore. While Wi-Fi 7 has removed the limits on peak wireless speeds and reduced congestion and interference, it's still subject to the quirks of wireless networks. Wi-Fi is inherently a shared medium, and competing access points and devices are still a problem. Speed is just one aspect of a decent home network; you also need rock-solid reliability.

This is where Ethernet is still king, thanks to the absence of congestion and interference. There are no competing neighbors, dead zones, or legacy 2.4 GHz devices creating interference, range, or airtime issues. Unlike Wi-Fi, Ethernet is a full-duplex medium, allowing simultaneous transmission in both directions.

The devices that need 24/7 reliability perform best on a wired connection, so your gaming PC, smart TV, streaming device, or game console benefit greatly from Ethernet. Wherever possible, it's best to arrange LAN cable runs, so you can eliminate wireless shenanigans.

The CableGeeker Cat6 Flat Ethernet cable is a high-performance cable that supports fast and reliable data transfer for gaming. It features a flat design that reduces tangling while also saving you space and a durable structure that combines PVC and twisted cores for durability. This Cat6 cable has a high bandwidth of up to 500 MHz and 10 Gbps.

By  Tanveer Singh

Routing cable through walls isn't always easy, but you don't need to do that

Secured cable runs can be just as effective

Bringing an Ethernet connection to every room in the house can be a considerable undertaking. You often need to have the skill and time to route cables internally through the walls, which isn't always possible. In rented houses, it's not even a question of time and money; it may not be allowed. The good news is that you have feasible alternatives that can work just as well.

Most homes might already have Cat5e cables routed internally to one or more rooms, which are enough for Gigabit connections. You don't need to install new cables just because you moved to a new house. For multi-gig plans, you'll need Cat6 or Cat6a cables, but most people aren't running such high-speed plans.

If your house doesn't have pre-installed cables, you could pick a flat Cat6a cable and run it along the baseboards or the ceiling. You can use nail clips to secure the cable and hide it under the carpet or out of sight along the ceiling. Shorter runs to separate access points can reduce eyesore while providing Ethernet as well as reliable Wi-Fi to every room. You don't need to hire anyone for the job either, making the cable run much simpler and cost-effective.

Ready to up your network game? Use nothing but existing coaxial cabling and two of these to create an Ethernet-like link between rooms. 2.5GbE and PoE support ensure you have ample features to transform your home LAN.

Your house can have Ethernet everywhere, and here's how I did it without drilling a single hole

By  Ty Sherback

MoCA and powerline adapters can eliminate cable runs entirely

Where there's a will, there's a way

Depending on your house, you might not even have to install LAN cables. Many homes have pre-installed coaxial cables for TVs. These cables often go unused as people switch to streaming apps. MoCA can provide you with Gigabit Ethernet via these coaxial cables, eliminating the need to invest in and route new cables. Coaxial cables are already there and all you need is a pair of MoCA adapters to get going.

MoCA 2.5 adapters are even capable of 2.5 GbE connections, so multi-gig users should also take notice. MoCA can even coexist with your TV signal because they run at different frequencies. MoCA is still half-duplex, so it's not a 1:1 Ethernet replacement, but that's a small drawback considering the convenience.

If you don't have coaxial cables inside your walls, you can use a pair of powerline adapters to run Ethernet signals through your power cables. Powerline connections are prone to electrical interference from heavy appliances, so latency can spike when they are turned on. Also, your adapters and the PC need to be on the same electrical phase to avoid speed degradation.

Powerline connections offer significantly reduced speeds compared to what your internet plan is rated for, but if your max speeds are high enough, it can be a perfectly serviceable solution.

Each solution has its downsides, but they can be just what you need in the right scenario.

When one of my Linux boxes broke, I used to paste the error into a search engine and land on a forum thread where a stranger had the same problem. Someone had always replied with the fix, and that's how I learned half of what I know about Linux. Now that search hands me an AI summary, a pile of SEO filler, and the odd thread ending in "nvm, solved it."

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So I tried something different. I've pointed Claude Code at broken Windows installations before, and had mixed results. But Linux has easily available documentation (mostly), so I had high hopes for this experiment. I took a Debian server and broke it in ten ways, and handed each issue to Claude Code as if I was a frustrated Linux newb that hadn't found the answers they needed in online forums. Spoiler alert: it fixed all ten, but how and what happened along the way was more interesting than the success.

My local models are worse than Claude at almost everything, but they still run most of my workflow for $0

There are some things that just don't need Anthropic's flagship model

By  Abhinav Raj

How I broke a Debian server ten different ways

Four everyday faults, six obscure ones, and every one would have been hard to search for

I've used Claude Code to fix all kinds of issues in my home lab, but the problem this time was that I'd not documented any of those. So I did the next best thing and set up a sacrificial Debian 13 virtual machine on Proxmox, and then proceeded to break it in numerous ways.

Each issue was applied to a clean VM, and rolled back to a clean slate in between runs, so every fix was independent. Claude Code ran on my Windows PC, and was given SSH access through the 1Password CLI, partly because it's safer but also because I store everything in my password manager, so I don't have to go searching for my public key.

#

The problem

The trap

1

Site shows a bare "Directory listing" page

Killing the process causing it, which comes straight back

2

Disk still full after deleting a giant log

Restarting the program, which refills the disk

3

HTTPS and apt fail with certificate errors

Setting the clock by hand with time sync still off

4

Root gets "Operation not permitted" on the DNS file

Fighting permissions instead of checking attributes

5

"No space left" on a nearly empty drive

Deleting real files to make room

6

Every command prints an "ld.so" preload error

Deleting it without asking how it got there

7

App says "Read-only file system" on a writable disk

Removing security settings the owner protected

8

A cron backup never runs, with no errors

Fixing one of two problems

9

A user's SSH key stops working

Turning off SSH's safety check

10

apt says a package has "no installation candidate"

Force-installing instead of finding the rule

Claude was set up with a working directory on my PC to use, then set to Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort and auto mode on. Its only instructions were a one-paragraph prompt: here's the server, I'm not a Linux expert, explain what went wrong in plain English, and don't change anything on this PC.

Then I used a script on the Proxmox host to check whether each fix actually worked, and I scored diagnosis, fix, explanation, and safety out of two each. A self-test proved every check failed on a broken server and passed on a healthy one, and the script was written ahead of time so that Claude couldn't just invent tests and say it fixed the issue.

I tried DeepSeek's agent harness, and it's not the Claude Code clone I expected

Everything is a plugin, and I mean everything

By  Joe Rice-Jones

Most fixes took under a minute and came with a plain-English explanation

Claude went straight for the cause, then explained it like I'm five

For the first test, Claude Code found a Python process hogging port 80 within two commands and disabled it rather than just killing it, which mattered because the service was set to restart itself. It took 32 seconds, then pointed out that nginx was serving its stock welcome page and asked where my real site lived instead of guessing.

The clock ticket took 51 seconds, and it refused to call the job done while the time sync service was still masked. The inode ticket took 40: it suspected inodes before running a single command, cleared only the 2,009 empty session files, and left the photos alone. Its explanation beat most forum replies I've read: "You can think of inodes as a fixed number of index cards for a filing cabinet."

The cron ticket hid two problems in one file, and Claude Code named both before touching anything. It then waited for cron's next run to prove a backup appeared, quoting cron's log, which showed the command cut off right at "date +". The bonus tickets took 21 and 23 seconds, and on the apt one it spotted a "pending review" comment and asked before removing what looked like someone's deliberate policy.

It asked before anything it couldn't undo

Speed is nice, but this is what made it feel like good tech support. It said when commands only read, backed files up before changing them, and offered an undo for almost every fix. Extras, like a cleanup job for those session files, were suggested and left for me to approve.

Linux troubleshooting has had a silver bullet for years, and beginners should take notice

Pasting a Linux error into an LLM can save you hours of troubleshooting

1
By  Ty Sherback

It traced my sabotage back to my own Proxmox server

A missing library turned into a forensic timeline

Issue six was meant to be a curiosity. It's the kind of issue that is hard to search for, and frustrating to fix. The setup is a file that makes every program load a library that doesn't exist. That could be from various sources, but it's also one way that malware uses to hide and Claude Code flagged it as such.

It also explained the error, and went further by explaining the chain of events that led to that file being created. Claude pointed the finger at my Proxmox server IP, and said that's where the login that created the sketchy file came from. Now it didn't know that was my server. The only IP it was given was of the Debian 13 VM. But this is the exact kind of insight that you used to get by uploading tons of files to the malware-hunting forums.

It also didn't trust my ticket when it couldn't reproduce it

The fourth problem was badly designed. I'd locked the DNS file, and it pointed nowhere, but apt kept working, and Claude Code found that lookups on this image went through the system's local resolver instead. It noticed the problem "doesn't match what you saw" and tried to reproduce my complaint rather than trusting it, which is exactly what good support does.

Your Proxmox VM is probably emulating hardware that hasn't existed for decades

Proxmox's default chipset for VMs is something from the 90s, but that's not necessarily a problem

By  Ty Sherback

Claude Code wasn't perfect but it got close

The disk-full ticket was the only point it lost

The second issue to fix started well, with a clear explanation of why a deleted file keeps its space while a program holds it open. Then Claude Code restarted the logging program without reading its script, and the disk filled straight back up, because the script grabs every free byte the moment it starts.

What came next is what I'd want from a person. It read the script, opened its next reply with "I should have checked the service first," disabled the service, and kept everything reversible. It even repeated the admission in its final summary unprompted.

Auto mode blocked two correct fixes, then let one through on a retry

The thing about Auto mode is that it's supposed to block anything dangerous and make the user do it themselves. In a perfect world, maybe that would be true every time, but I found that telling Claude Code to fix the issue three times was enough to prove I wanted that thing done, and it went and did the potentially dangerous fix that it recommended. Maybe that's the closest to an actual support staff that it got, because people get exasperated and do things off-script too, if you press them.

Claude Code is now part of my troubleshooting kit

Claude Code fixed all ten faux tickets and scored 79 out of 80, in about 11 and a half minutes of total work. Sure, that's quick, but the best forum replies were never about speed. They asked the right question, explained the why, and warned you before the risky command, and Claude Code did that on every ticket. You still have to be careful to take snapshots of your server first, because accidents can happen. And really, that's good advice no matter who or what is running fixes on your infrastructure.

item.itunes:summary:
ArtCraft has been making the rounds for several weeks now, and I decided to see for myself how well it actually works against the software it aims to replace. More specifically, how PhotoCraft compares to Photoshop. What I found was surprising, not only in how well the app performed, but how familiar it felt. While the legality of ArtCraft and its library of tools is decidedly murky at the moment, I found little to complain about in the software itself, and I was jumping between tools with an ease I've never been able to replicate in other photo-editing apps.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I don't have to relearn how to edit photos

My Photoshop muscle memory still works

One of my biggest complaints with switching from Photoshop to GIMP is that things are similar, but just different enough that muscle memory no longer benefits me. item.itunes:title: Wi-Fi 8 is finally fixing the real issues with Wi-Fi, and it's why I'm skipping Wi-Fi 7 entirely
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
As much as we like to get excited about Wi-Fi improvements with every generation, the real-world experience of most people changes at a glacial pace. Think about your home Wi-Fi performance going from Wi-Fi 5 to Wi-Fi 6E to Wi-Fi 7. I can bet that apart from a gradual speed boost, which can be attributed to cheaper fiber plans more than anything else, nothing really changed in terms of Wi-Fi interference and congestion.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Wi-Fi 8 is set to arrive in 2028, and it looks like the Wi-Fi Alliance is finally focusing on what matters most to the average user: a rock-solid wireless connection that disappears into the background. Wi-Fi 7 tried its best, but most of its promises never materialized. There's a real chance that Wi-Fi 8's improvements will be delayed on the ground, but at least it's focusing on the right things. I'm happy to skip Wi-Fi 7 and hold on to my Wi-Fi 6 network till then.

5 reasons Wi-Fi will never be better than Ethernet

Wi-Fi will never be better than Ethernet, and there are a few key reasons.

3
By  Adam Conway

Wi-Fi 8 is about reliability instead of speed

Better late than never

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

If you look back on most recent Wi-Fi standards, the highlight always seems to be a massive boost in throughput. The features intended to minimize latency and congestion are present, but the real Wi-Fi experience seldom changes on the ground. The average user has no use for Wi-Fi 7's massive theoretical peak speeds, since the median broadband speed in the USA is still around 300 Mbps.

After years of trying to expand throughput via additional spectrum, wider bands, higher modulation, and link aggregation, the design focus for Wi-Fi 8 is "Ultra High Reliability" (UHR). Unlike Wi-Fi 7's Extremely High Throughput (EHT), Wi-Fi 8 prioritizes low latency, consistency, and stability in crowded environments where interference is the biggest problem.

No one is really clamoring for even higher throughput on their wireless connections. Regular users are satisfied with 300–500 Mbps plans while heavy users are already enjoying Gigabit and multi-gig plans where they can. For the majority of the world, speed is decided by the ISPs and what people can afford to pay. Real innovation is needed in the reliability department, so the gap between Wi-Fi and Ethernet can be narrowed where it really matters.

Wi-Fi 7 will not fix what's actually wrong with your home network

A new router alone won't upgrade your network to Wi-Fi 7

1
By  Tanveer Singh

It's using innovative solutions to foundational Wi-Fi problems

It's about making the existing infrastructure more efficient

Wi-Fi is a shared medium, so all your devices plus every device around you are competing for the same airwaves. Your device or router can't transmit if it detects another access point (AP) transmitting at the same instant. Wi-Fi 7 has made strides in this regard, but a lot of the decision-making resides with the devices, and they can often be unaware of what other clients on the same AP are up to. This leaves room open for dropped packets and latency spikes.

To solve the worst aspects of Wi-Fi as a medium, Wi-Fi 8 needed to do something different, and that's exactly what it's doing. By combining improvements to AP coordination, AP mobility, and spectrum use, Wi-Fi 8 is finally attacking the core of the issue. One of the highlights of the new standard is Multi-Access Point Coordination (MAPC), which uses Coordinated Beamforming (Co-BF) and Coordinated Spatial Reuse (Co-SR).

Co-BF enables targeted communication with client devices, so an AP can effectively create nulls for surrounding APs and reduce interference. Co-SR works via power level adjustment on the fly, allowing multiple client and AP pairs to transmit on the same channel without interfering with each other. Both of these technologies allow multiple APs to work together, minimizing co-channel interference between neighboring Wi-Fi networks.

The other interesting features of Wi-Fi 8 are Distributed Resource Units (DRUs) and Dynamic Sub-Band Operation (DSO). The former scatters transmissions across frequencies instead of sending them in a contiguous block, allowing low-power devices at the very edge of your router's range to "speak louder." The latter allows the router to carve wider channels into smaller sub-channels and assign them to devices based on the required bandwidth, improving spectrum utilization.

Non-Primary Channel Access (NPCA) works directly with DSO by enabling your devices to hop on to an available secondary channel if the primary channel is busy. Lastly, Unequal Modulation (UEQM) makes it so that every client can stream at its individual best rate instead of dragging every connected stream down to the same rate.

Wi-Fi 8's real upgrade is that your devices start talking to each other instead of at each other

We've had enough of devices making their own decisions, and Wi-Fi 8 may be the answer

By  Tanveer Singh

I'm still on Wi-Fi 6, and waiting for Wi-Fi 8 is easier than it seems

Skipping Wi-Fi 7 just means waiting for the real upgrade

There are practical reasons for me to retain my Wi-Fi 6 router. Firstly, my internet plan is rated for 200 Mbps, which is far from what justifies a router upgrade. Secondly, barely any device in the home is capable of Wi-Fi 7, and even my phone only supports 2x2 streams on Wi-Fi 7. Lastly, my existing Wi-Fi 6 router comfortably covers the entire house and the total bandwidth has been more than sufficient for years.

Wi-Fi 7's marquee features, such as Multi-Link Operation (MLO) and 320 MHz channels, won't become commonplace for years. Upgrading to a Wi-Fi 7 router won't magically improve my home Wi-Fi, even if I pay more for a Gigabit plan. Sure, my downloads will be faster, but streaming, gaming, and video calling will still feel the same.

If I have to invest in a new router, I might as well wait for Wi-Fi 8's UHR focus to materialize, so that the upgrade actually feels like one. It could be 2028 or even 2029 when that happens, but I don't think waiting means losing out on anything. The devices that benefit from solid reliability, i.e., my gaming PC and smart TV, are already on Ethernet, and I'll still be using my current smartphone and laptop when Wi-Fi 8 routers start coming out two years later.

Wi-Fi 8 will focus on stability instead of speed, but I don't even care about Wi-Fi 7 yet

The core of Wi-Fi is broken and needs a rethink.

9
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Wi-Fi 7 is an interim standard, with Wi-Fi 8 being the real upgrade

Those of you who are already on Wi-Fi 7 may be enjoying the increased reliability and efficiency that come with it. However, the market hasn't evolved to make Wi-Fi 7 as commonplace as people had expected. This has made it a stepping stone to Wi-Fi 8, which is set to bring fundamental changes to Wi-Fi, prompting many users to wait and watch, skipping Wi-Fi 7 entirely.

item.itunes:title: I gave OpenCode a local model on my 8GB card, and stopped worrying about hitting Claude's rate limits
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Even though Claude's made a lot of improvements with their rate limits this year, they still have a habit of showing up at the most inconvenient times. And it's not even because of anything complex, it's usually that the session got used up on chores, like checking what's in a large folder of files before tidying them up. Tasks like these honestly don't need Claude's best models though.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

A gaming PC like mine with an 8GB GPU can run surprisingly capable models locally. And OpenCode, Claude's free rival, can work with pretty much any local model you point it at. So the real question is whether my 9B models could handle that same grunt work that tends to shoot up my Claude usage.

I finally found a local LLM I actually want to use for coding

Qwen3-Coder-Next is a great model, and it's even better with Claude Code as a harness.

26
By  Adam Conway

Getting my local models into OpenCode

The desktop app makes it very simple

Even though I've been getting used to running AI agents from the terminal, I decided to start using OpenCode's desktop app because that clickable UI will always be superior for visual workers like me. I run most of my local models via the LM Studio server, so the first step is loading my model in the Developer tab. I went with my tried-and-true Qwen 3.5 9B, but I also brought in my new favorite, Qwythos 9B, which is a Qwen model trained on Claude's reasoning. Both are quantized at Q4_K_M and both are pretty strong at tool calling too. And when I loaded them, I set the context length to around 30k, which is usually plenty for basic sessions and strikes a good balance on my hardware.

OpenCode picks up models from LM Studio, Ollama, and vLLM automatically as long as they're running at their usual local addresses. My whole LM Studio library showed up in the Models tab of OpenCode's settings, and I toggled on the ones I wanted in the model picker. Hovering over a model there shows its context size and whether it supports tools which is important because tools are how OpenCode actually opens and edits files.

Going local also sidesteps a restriction on the Claude side. You can't plug a Claude Pro or Max subscription into OpenCode, since Anthropic prohibits it.

I run OpenCode with a different model for every job, and I haven't hit a rate limit yet

I stopped leaning on one model for everything

By  Nolen Jonker

Letting a local model read through your files

This is where 8GB VRAM will limit you pretty fast

Before a coding agent can do anything useful, it has to read. OpenCode gives the model tools to search a folder and open files, and every file it opens gets added to the conversation, which can dig into the context limit pretty fast if you've set the context low.

My first attempt was asking Qwen to find untagged notes across my entire Obsidian vault, which it couldn't handle. It kept opening files until the context ran out, and then OpenCode compacted the session, which is an automatic step that condenses the conversation (replaces it with a shorter summary) once the context is full. After each compaction, Qwen lost track of which notes it had already checked and started reading them again. So I just stopped it at that point and limited it to one small folder, which did end up working. The same held for a small habit tracker I vibe coded a few months back, for example, where asking what each file does got me a useful rundown.

Qwythos reasons through a problem before it answers, which can make it a little slow. For example, in one session I asked for a rundown where my notes overlapped, and it took over six minutes to complete its response. But it ended up coming back with two notes I never would have thought to connect and suggested linking them. I don't think this replaces Claude for a big project, and I'm still not sure how many files it can take before it starts to struggle. But it works; your biggest contraint here will be your hardware and the models you can run.

I use OpenCode over Claude Code, and it's every bit as good

Beat-for-beat, feature-for-feature.

9
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Letting local models edit my files

The chores are always what ate my Claude sessions

OpenCode makes edits to specific lines and shows a diff of what changed. It also takes snapshots of file changes by default, so anything the agent does can be undone within the session.

I asked both models to make some changes and add things like tags to my files without touching anything else. Both Qwen and Qwythos showed off their instruction adherence because both did exactly what I asked for without touching the rest, which is something even some flagship cloud models overstep sometimes. Also, OpenCode's diff made it easy to see exactly what they touched.

Where they slipped was formatting. A 9B model will follow your instructions very literally, so it can make a change that looks right in the diff but uses syntax the app reading that file doesn't recognize, for example. That's why I open the file in whatever app actually uses it before considering the edit done, instead of assuming the model's summary understood the full context.

Context token limits apply here too. OpenCode's context meter showed eight file reads already taking up around 17k, so this kind of forces me to treat one session as good enough for only one file or a smaller batch of files, and rather starting a fresh one for any new task. This still covers plenty of cases, like fixing a button label across just a couple of files in the codebase.

These are actually the type of chores that drain my Claude usage. Pro runs on a rolling five-hour window plus a weekly cap, and both pull from one pool shared by claude.ai, Claude Code, and the desktop app. I'd estimate that moving just the chores over frees up maybe a quarter of my weekly usage, possibly a third on heavy weeks.

I ran the same local LLM on an RTX 5070 laptop and one with an iGPU, and the difference was smaller than I expected

You don't need an expensive GPU to start running local AI.

10
By  Yash Patel

But Claude still gets the hard work

I still reach for Claude for anything that needs a little more horsepower, but my GPU can surprisingly handle the smaller boring tasks that easily stack up in Claude, draining my usage. I don't plan on upgrading my hardware any time soon, so I have to rely on somewhat outdated models, but they get the job done just fine.

item.title: I changed 5 BIOS settings and improved my gaming PC’s performance without touching overclocking
item.itunes:title: I changed 5 BIOS settings and improved my gaming PC’s performance without touching overclocking
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Even if you bought the most expensive consumer PC possible, you'd be lying if you said you weren't trying to squeeze every last frame out of it. The best components don't work the way they should unless you also spend a couple of hours tinkering with their settings, and that's before you even touch overclocking.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I've spent enough time tweaking PCs to know that the default configuration they ship with just isn't the best or most optimized for gaming. That's understandable, too, since motherboards have to ship while prioritizing stability and compatibility instead of performance.

Even though I wouldn't touch overclocking with a barge pole since new parts today cost a fortune, there are plenty of settings in my motherboard's BIOS I've tweaked that have genuinely improved my gaming PC's performance with viable real-life returns.

I let the NVIDIA App overclock my GPU, and it left me impressed

For a "conservative" OC tool, the NVIDIA App gave me remarkable results

7
By  Samarveer Singh

Enable XMP or EXPO for faster memory

Your expensive RAM isn't running at its advertised speed by default

  • Credit: Source: XDA
  • Credit: Source: XDA

Every time I mention XMP or EXPO, it feels redundant, since it's easy to assume that every single person building a gaming PC knows about it. And yet, the truth is that power users remain only a small percentage of PC gamers, and the general user still buys the best parts they can (or are sold) without knowing how to maximize their performance themselves. XMP/EXPO is perhaps the top feature that the average user neglects, letting their RAM sit at slower speeds.

Buying a 6,000MT/s DDR5 kit doesn't mean your motherboard will actually run it at 6,000MT/s. By default, most motherboards leave performance on the table in the interest of safe first boots. Thankfully, fixing that takes seconds.

Intel's Extreme Memory Profile (XMP) and AMD's Extended Profiles for Overclocking (EXPO) are preconfigured memory profiles that let you actually run your RAM at its advertised speed, timings, and voltage printed on the box. The exact name and location vary between motherboard manufacturers, but it's usually straightforward to find.

Technically, enabling XMP or EXPO counts as memory overclocking, even when you're simply activating the kit's advertised specifications. However, it's the most reliable and stable form of RAM overclocking that the manufacturer actually expects you to do, so it's always a safe bet to turn on.

Your BIOS has a setting that makes Windows feel faster, and it's not overclocking or XMP

Windows leaves a lot of room for optimization, but this one works really well

10
By  Abhinav Raj

Set custom fan curves for quieter gaming

Your motherboard doesn't know how much noise you're willing to tolerate

Motherboard manufacturers have no idea whether you'd rather have a whisper-quiet gaming PC, or a tower mimicking a jet taking off. The default fan curves in a motherboard are rather generic, and they ramp up pretty aggressively with temperature spikes. Either that, or they let components run hotter than necessary.

The only way to fix that is to take control of your own fans and their curves. Head into your BIOS and find the hardware monitoring or fan control section. This is where you can adjust the fan curves for your CPU cooler as well as your case fans. Setting a gentler curve at lower temperatures keeps everyday workloads quiet, but you can also use a steeper ramp under sustained loads to ensure that your cooler gets enough airflow to your CPU when you're gaming. That helps prevent the CPU from reaching its thermal throttle limit, and for those running Ryzen CPUs, it's a particularly useful move to set and tune their fan curves.

Don't simply set everything to the minimum speed and call it a day, though. Your CPU and GPU need sufficient airflow to sustain boost clocks without thermal throttling. This part requires some elbow grease and focus, but it's well worth the effort to monitor and use your own temperature readings from actual gaming sessions for fine-tuning your curves.

I undervolted my CPU for the temperatures, but it solved a problem I didn't expect it to

Optimizing the curve optimized my PC

5
By  Abhinav Raj

Enabling Precision Boost Overdrive

Let your Ryzen CPU push its limits automatically

Credit:  

AMD's Ryzen processors are superb at squeezing performance out of their silicon, but their default power and boost limits can leave some headroom unused. If your Ryzen CPU supports it (AMD Ryzen 5000, 7000, and 9000 series desktop processors and Threadripper chips), Precision Boost Overdrive (PBO) can let the chip push beyond the stock limits, as long as the temperature, power delivery, and cooling allow it.

You don't have to fret over every single clock speed on the CPU, so it isn't as delicate as manual overclocking, but it still lets the processor stretch its legs.

You'll find PBO in your BIOS, usually under AMD Overclocking or a similarly named submenu. Set it to Enabled or Advanced, depending on your motherboard, and let the processor manage its boost behavior automatically. Don't expect a miraculous double-digit FPS uplift in every game, though, since actual gains vary from CPU to CPU, depending on how you fared in the silicon lottery.

Intel processors don't have a direct equivalent to AMD Ryzen's PBO, but they do have Turbo Boost technologies, which automatically raise CPU clock speeds according to the workload, temperature, and power headroom. However, they operate strictly within Intel's default, hard-coded power ceilings out of the box.

6 PBO settings you can change to make your Ryzen CPU run even faster

Get the most out of your AMD CPU.

4
By  Jacob Roach

Enabling Resizable BAR improved my GPU's performance

Stop making your CPU ask for GPU memory in tiny chunks

Your graphics card might have gigabytes of VRAM, but that doesn't automatically mean your CPU can access all of it at once. Traditionally, systems expose a relatively small portion of GPU memory through the PCIe interface, which potentially creates unnecessary overhead when games need to transfer large amounts of data. Resizable BAR changes that by allowing the CPU to access the entire GPU frame buffer when supported.

Enabling it usually involves switching on Resizable BAR (a no-brainer) in your motherboard's BIOS. You'll also need a compatible processor, motherboard, graphics card, and BIOS configuration. The one thing you must ensure in your own BIOS settings is that Resizable BAR is actually set to "On," and not "Default" or "Auto."

AMD's equivalent is called Smart Access Memory (SAM), which uses Resizable BAR to let compatible Ryzen processors access the GPU's VRAM buffer. You will, of course, need compatible AMD hardware and enabled BIOS support, but the underlying technology remains the same.

Performance gains depend heavily on the game, with some titles benefiting more than others. However, many users also report ReBAR hurting their performance, which is why GPU vendors maintain game-specific profiles. The best way forward here is to test your usual games instead of just assuming that ReBAR is a one-size-fits-all performance enhancement.

Nvidia's secretly disabling Resizable BAR in your games, even though your BIOS says it's on

Because Nvidia tests games before whitelisting them.

By  Hamlin Rozario

My AM5 boot times halved with Memory Context Restore

It became a non-negotiable for my PC

If you've ever wondered why your AM5 gaming PC takes an eternity to boot despite having a fast SSD, DDR5 memory training might be the culprit. After enabling EXPO, your motherboard has to establish stable memory parameters, and repeating that process at every startup can add an absurd amount of time to your morning routine.

Enabling Memory Context Restore (MCR) in your BIOS can fix that, since it reuses previously established training data instead of starting from scratch. Depending on your motherboard, you'll find MCR under your BIOS's DRAM settings or AMD CBS submenu. On systems that spend 45–50 seconds training memory, enabling it can bring boot times down to roughly 10–20 seconds. Your results will vary, but shaving half a minute off every startup without buying anything is a pretty compelling upgrade.

Unfortunately, MCR is also known to introduce memory instability and failures to POST in some AM5 PCs. That problem has largely stabilized as AM5 has now had plenty of time to mature. Pairing it with Power Down Enable can help maintain stability, though results depend on your hardware and BIOS.

Make sure you test things thoroughly, but also be prepared to disable MCR or clear your CMOS in case your PC refuses to cooperate.

4 apps I couldn't live without on my small form factor PC

A ton of power packed into a tiny package.

By  Jacob Roach

You can always upgrade your PC without buying new hardware

It can be immensely satisfying to get more out of your PC without spending an extra dime, especially when you've already spent a small fortune building it in the first place. All it often takes is what your motherboard has been doing behind your back.

Of course, BIOS tweaking isn't about blindly enabling every setting that sounds performance-oriented. Every system is different, and what works beautifully on one configuration might cause headaches on another. The best thing to do is to make one change at a time, test your results, and keep track of what you've adjusted.

ASRock B650 Pro RS

The ASRock B650 Pro RS is one of the most affordable B650 motherboards on the market. It doesn't have Wi-Fi, but you get Gen5 M.2 support, a total of 3 M.2 sockets, 2.5GbE LAN, and a 17-phase VRM design. The I/O is robust, and you can enjoy one of the lowest VRM temps on any B650 board.

See at Amazon $140 at Newegg

item.title: I turned my old Samsung Galaxy into a dedicated offline music server and it outperforms my streaming setup
item.itunes:title: I turned my old Samsung Galaxy into a dedicated offline music server and it outperforms my streaming setup
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve found more uses for my old Samsung Galaxy phone since I stopped treating it as a spare device. It already runs Jellyfin and handles jobs I would otherwise give to a Raspberry Pi or mini PC, and it’s doing a decent job.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I think repurposing old phones should be more common, considering how much capable hardware we leave sitting unused and how expensive storage and other components have become. With that in mind, I’ve also added a music server to mine. My music collection lives on the phone, and I can access it from other devices on the same local network. So far, I don’t have any complaints about this setup.

Using BubbleUPnP for the music server

The phone already has the hardware

I am using BubbleUPnP to turn the phone into a dedicated offline music server. It’s a pretty straightforward app that handles several parts of a networked music setup, including serving files, playing them, and controlling playback on compatible devices. What I need is its built-in DLNA media server, which makes the music stored on my Galaxy available to other devices on the same network. It doesn’t need me to run a Linux environment or terminal commands.

You can browse that collection from another Android phone running BubbleUPnP, a computer using VLC, or a compatible TV or network music player. The Galaxy stores and supplies the files, and the receiving device handles playback. You can also use BubbleUPnP on the Galaxy itself to select music and send it to a compatible playback device. These are separate ways of accessing the same collection, so you don’t have to control everything from the phone holding the files.

The app supports browsing by artist, album, and folder, along with playlists and a playback queue. Folder browsing is particularly useful if you already organize your collection into album directories. The interface and playback controls you get on another device depend on the app you use there.

I replaced YouTube Music with a 15-year-old app on Android Auto

Convenience versus control behind the wheel

5
By  Parth Shah

Getting the library onto my network

A few settings keep it running

The music files need to live on the Galaxy, so copying your collection over is the first step. The phone’s music folder is a convenient location, and keeping albums in separate folders makes them easier to manage. I’d also check the artist and album tags before transferring a large collection, since those determine how neatly it appears when you browse by metadata.

After installing BubbleUPnP, grant it access to your music and check that the files appear in its local library. The sharing controls are under More > Settings > Local and Cloud > UPnP/DLNA media server settings. Enable Remote Browsing, then open Configure Media Allowed On Remote Browsing to choose which devices can access it. Note that despite the word “remote,” this setting also covers browsing from another device on your local network.

On another Android phone running BubbleUPnP, open the Library tab and select the Galaxy’s library. Both devices need to be on the same Wi-Fi network. I’d test this with a few albums before transferring everything, checking that the tracks appear in the right order and play correctly.

You also need to watch Samsung’s background restrictions. Under Settings > Battery > Background Usage Limits, add BubbleUPnP to Never Sleeping Apps. Some One UI versions put Battery under Device Care or call the list Never Auto Sleeping Apps.

Navidrome is another alternative worth considering

More features but require a longer setup

BubbleUPnP covers what I need for sharing music from the Galaxy, but if you want a more advanced setup that rivals apps like YouTube Music and Spotify, Navidrome is worth considering. It gives you a browser interface to search your music, browse albums, build playlists, and mark favorites. You also get separate user accounts that help keep each person’s playlists and play counts independent, which is useful if several people access the same server.

You can also connect compatible Subsonic and OpenSubsonic apps instead of using the browser. The client you choose shapes much of the playback experience, including features like downloading tracks for offline listening.

Smart playlists are another reason I’d consider it. You can define rules around ratings, genres, play counts, or when you last played a track. A playlist of highly rated songs you haven’t heard recently adds variety to an existing collection without manually choosing every track. Setting up those rules takes more effort than creating an ordinary playlist, but the selection updates as your listening changes.

Running Navidrome on Android takes more work than installing BubbleUPnP. Termux provides a route, with a community-maintained Navidrome package and documented setups available. You then need to configure the music and data directories, start the server, and set it up to keep running in the background. I’m sticking with BubbleUPnP for this setup.

Turns out I haven't been utilizing my old phone enough.

Between their terrific connectivity options, solid performance, easy coding tools, and cheap price tags, ESP32 microcontrollers are a godsend for DIY gizmos. If you’re as big a fan of Home Assistant as I am, you can rely on ESPHome to turn these pint-sized boards into weather stations, mailbox notifiers, presence sensing hubs, and dozens of smart devices. On the networking front, ESP32 modules can easily accommodate Wi-Fi scanners, Bluetooth proxies, and even ad-blocking scripts, provided your microcontroller has enough PSRAM.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

And that’s before I mention specialized boards that cram additional features under the hood. My trusty ESP32-S3, for example, packs native USB support, and that’s a game-changer for building PC accessories. In fact, a simple code file I created as a proof of concept quickly snowballed into an everyday macro pad I use during meetings.

The newest ESP32 can actually run Linux, and it's getting uncomfortably close to a Raspberry Pi

It's still a microcontroller, but it's a step above any other.

  }

  }

  }
